headline: Midnight Outgoing: The Deep Hole Behind the Rocks, and Weakfish Waking Up at Ponquogue
subhead: With the bay running warm and stripers going nocturnal, the smart money is on the tide after dark — and the bridge bite is finally worth the mosquito bites.
body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday night to skip the sunset bite entirely and wait for the tide to really start pulling — 11:40 outgoing, dead of night, nobody on the jetty but me and one guy from Riverhead who talks too much on the phone. That's the decision I keep making this time of year. When the bay's sitting in the high 70s like it is right now, the bass don't want anything to do with daylight. They slide into the deep water and wait for the sun to go down and the current to start moving bait past their nose. So that's where I put my hours.

The hole behind the north jetty rocks, the one that drops to eighteen, twenty feet on the last of the outgoing — that's been the address. I've been soaking bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig, 3 ounces of lead to hold bottom against that current, and I've also had good luck swimming a live eel along the rock face on a light egg sinker, just enough weight to keep it down without killing the action. Fish have been coming in the 26 to 34-inch range, mixed in with a few shorts, and every single one of them showed up in that window from an hour before low water through the first hour of the new incoming. Bite the tide change wrong and you're just chumming for sea robins. I watched three guys leave at 1 a.m. with nothing because they fished the wrong two hours — showed up at high water instead of low. Timing is everything out here right now, more than usual.

We flagged this last week — said the back bay was sitting warm, mid-to-upper 70s, and that the tide swing around the new moon would flush hard through the inlet. That's exactly what set this bite up. All that warm water pouring out on the ebb concentrates bait right at the inlet mouth and the current seams off the rocks, and the bass that have gone deep and lazy during the day get aggressive again once that flow really starts ripping after dark.

Ponquogue Bridge has been the other piece of good news, and honestly it surprised me a little. Weakfish have been showing up on calm, warm evenings — not every night, but when the wind lays down and the water goes glassy under the lights, guys are picking off weakfish in the 3 to 5 pound class drifting bucktails tipped with squid strips right along the pilings on the last two hours of the outgoing. Bloodworms on a simple hi-lo rig have worked too if you don't want to jig. It's not a blitz — you might get two or three fish in a session — but it's real, and it's the best that stretch has fished in a couple years. The bridge lights pull the bait, the bait pulls the weakfish, and the tide does the rest. I'd rather take three quality weakfish under those lights than grind out shorts anywhere else.

Daytime, the fluke have been the honest bite. Nothing spectacular, but dependable, which counts for something in mid-July heat. Drifting the inlet bar and the channel edge off the Coast Guard station, white and chartreuse Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails, has been putting keepers in the 18 to 21-inch range in the boat on the last of the incoming. Tiana Beach flats have given up a few doormats to guys drifting squid strips over the sandy patches, but you have to cover water — there's no one spot holding fish all day. The canal end, where the bay squeezes into that current toward the Peconic, has had some sneaky good fluke action too on the push tide, plus the occasional weakfish getting flushed through with the bait. Worth a drift if the main bay's slow.

Bluefish have been more rumor than reality here so far — plenty of snappers in the bay, and a few cocktail blues mixed in with the bass on the rocks at night, but nothing like the bunker blitzes tearing up the beaches to the west. If that bait moves east, and there's a decent chance it does if this calm weather holds, Shinnecock could see its own version of that show. I wouldn't count on it yet, but I'd keep a bag of metal in the truck just in case.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward first quarter on the 21st, so the current should start softening up through the weekend. That usually means slower presentations pay off better — smaller bucktails, lighter drifts, less horsing the tide. If I had one night to fish this week, I'd still take the midnight outgoing at the inlet rocks over anything in daylight. The bass are there, they're just waiting for the lights to go out and the water to start moving. Bring bug spray, bring patience, and don't show up at the wrong end of the tide.
